samples.text:
The graph shows the average time that people spent to commute one way in four cities, City A, B, C and D, from 2004 to 2024.

In 2004 City D had the longest commuting time with 45 minutes and City C had the shortest with 22 minutes. City A was 38 minutes and City B was 29 minutes.

City A increased steadily and in 2016 it was 52 minutes, which was the longest on the graph. City C also increased a lot, from 22 to 40 minutes in 2016. However, City D decreased every year and it was 37 minutes in 2016. City B did not change much, it was about 30 minutes.

In 2020, all four cities had a fall. For example City A dropped to 41 minutes and City B dropped to 25 minutes. After that, commuting times was going up again in 2024. City A was 49 minutes, City C was 44 minutes, City D was 33 and City B was 31.

Overall, City A and C got longer commuting time, City D got shorter and City B was stable, also all of them decreased in 2020.
samples.why: Overview placed at the end and loosely linked · key features covered with some list-like detail · limited cohesive range · collocation, agreement and comma splice errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The line graph provides information about the average time taken to commute one way in four cities between 2004 and 2024.

Overall, commuting times rose noticeably in City A and City C, while City D's fell and City B's remained fairly stable. Another clear feature is that every city experienced a drop in 2020, followed by an increase in 2024.

In 2004, City D had the longest average commute at 45 minutes, followed by City A (38 minutes), City B (29 minutes) and City C (22 minutes). Over the next twelve years, commuting times in City A increased steadily to 52 minutes, and City C's also grew rapidly, reaching 40 minutes in 2016. By contrast, the figure for City D declined gradually to 37 minutes, meaning that it was overtaken by both of them.

City B, however, changed very little during this time, ranging between 29 and 33 minutes. In 2020 all four cities saw shorter commutes, with City B recording the lowest figure of 25 minutes. By 2024, times had risen again, with City A at 49 minutes, City C at 44 minutes, which was double its 2004 figure, and City B and City D at 31 and 33 minutes respectively.
samples.why: Clear overview of diverging trends and the 2020 dip · key features well highlighted · logical organisation · range of cohesive devices, with slight overuse of 'with' structures · largely error-free.

samples.text:
The graph compares the average length of a one-way commute in Cities A, B, C and D over the twenty years from 2004 to 2024.

Overall, the cities followed different long-term trends: commuting times lengthened considerably in City A and City C, contracted in City D and changed little in City B. All four, however, saw a temporary reduction in 2020, and City A ended the period with the longest commute.

In 2004, commuters in City D faced the longest journeys, at 45 minutes, whereas those in City C had the shortest, at just 22 minutes. Over the following twelve years, City A's average rose steadily from 38 to a peak of 52 minutes, and City C's climbed even more steeply to 40 minutes. City D moved in the opposite direction, falling to 37 minutes, so that by 2016 it had been overtaken by both. City B, meanwhile, remained remarkably consistent at around half an hour.

In 2020, times dropped across the board, most noticeably in City A, where they fell by 11 minutes to 41. The subsequent rebound left City A on 49 minutes and City C on 44, twice its initial figure, while City B returned to 31 minutes and City D edged up to 33.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, including crossovers and the 2020 dip · clear, well-placed overview · accurate figures and derived comparisons · precise, flexible vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
